A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching central architectures, theorems and proof appendices. All 21 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2 are readable; v2 retains Appendices A–E and adds Appendices F–G.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical results, proofs and implementation suggestions, but no original experimental or data-analysis outcomes, including in its appendices.

after.justification: Appendix G reports original two-moon and MNIST classification experiments, including test accuracies and weight-normalization timings in Tables 1–3.

M1.justification: The central ReLU architectures are retained. Appendix F.3 introduces a composite-activation variant using f(s) = u1^T sigma(u2 s + u3) inside residual blocks. Appendix G also evaluates adaptations with unconstrained input layers and, for MNIST, an unconstrained ten-dimensional output layer.

E1.justification: v1 has no empirical dataset coverage. v2 adds classification on two-moon data with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.1 and on MNIST. Adversarial robustness and inverse problems remain motivating applications rather than evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 newly compare the architecture associated with Theorem 4.1 against that associated with Theorem 3.1 on two-moon classification. This is a limited comparison between the two retained architecture families; MNIST evaluates only the Theorem 4.1 variant, and cited external studies are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix G introduces experimental protocols absent from v1: 4,000 two-moon points with a stated 20% training fraction, the standard MNIST split with normalized inputs, batch size 256, Adam and cosine scheduling. It specifies depth/width sweeps, test accuracy and mean per-epoch normalization time, while explicitly relaxing input-layer constraints and MNIST output-layer constraints.

E4.justification: v2 adds empirical sensitivity analyses of depth at fixed width and width at fixed depth on two-moon data, plus a width-by-depth MNIST study. Tables 1–2 also examine normalization overhead across configurations. No corresponding empirical analyses appear in v1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, independent training-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's averaging of normalization time over epochs defines its timing metric rather than providing run-to-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: v2 adds all empirical result entries in Tables 1–3. For example, Table 1 reports 99.75% versus 88.25% accuracy for the Theorem 3.1 and 4.1 variants at width 5 and depth 2; at depth 64 both reach 100%, with normalization times of 0.1628 and 0.685 seconds. MNIST accuracies range from 97.58% to 97.94%. These are newly reported results, not improvements over v1 measurements.

T1.justification: The original theorems and proofs in Appendices A–E remain unchanged. v2 nevertheless adds substantial formal material: an exact function-class characterization in Remark 4.1, a logarithmic-depth parallel-max construction in F.2, a density argument for composite nonpolynomial activations in F.3, and an orthogonal-Jacobian derivation in G. F.1 also introduces a Banach fixed-point statement whose stated condition lacks a uniform contraction factor below one.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions retain the same scalar universality, exact piecewise-affine representation, fixed-width d+3 architecture and practical implementability claims. The added paragraph in Section 1.2 emphasizes the existing constructive proof strategy; the new experiments support an already stated practical claim.

C2.justification: Appendices F–G substantially expand interpretation and applicability qualifications. They explain that constructive size bounds need not be efficient, discuss difficulties enforcing Lipschitz constraints with other activations, interpret the normalization overhead, and acknowledge that MNIST's vector output does not directly match the scalar theoretical results. Application mechanisms involving margins and iterative reconstruction are also developed.

D1.justification: v1 offers high-level projection, power-method and regularization suggestions. Appendix G adds PyTorch and GPU information, optimizer and batch details, a proposed dynamical-isometry initialization, and multiple initial power iterations followed by one per gradient step. It also supplies a code-repository link, although learning rates, epoch counts and seeds remain unspecified in the PDF.

R1.justification: v2 adds ten references supporting expanded discussion of graph networks, attention, plug-and-play methods, ReLU approximation and dynamical isometry. The central positioning relative to GroupSort, spline networks and prior constrained ResNets remains intact; most existing citation changes are renumbering.

P1.justification: The original section order, proof organization and nearly all existing prose are retained. v2 adds a contribution-explanation paragraph, cross-references, Remark 4.1 and Appendices F–G, alongside small affiliation and publication-header edits. There is no extensive rewriting of the retained narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds three compact tables: two paired accuracy/timing comparisons and one MNIST width-by-depth grid. v1 has no such displays. The single-column mathematical layout is retained, with local reflow and a conference footer rather than a broader visual redesign.

improvement.justification: Appendix G adds useful practical support for v1's implementability claims through experiments, implementation instructions and a code-access statement, while the central proofs are preserved. The benefit is limited: relaxed experimental constraints prevent direct validation of the exact constrained models, uncertainty is unreported, and F.1 introduces an incorrect Banach condition by substituting pointwise strict distance decrease for uniform contraction. The practical and reproducibility gains therefore constitute a modest improvement rather than a substantial increase in rigor.
